division.heading: Actions Started by Statement of Claim

subdivision.heading: Time Limit for Service of Statement of Claim

operative_text.controlling:
3.27(1)  The Court may, at any time, grant an extension of time for
service of a statement of claim in any of the following
circumstances:
(a) if a defendant, anyone purporting to be a defendant, or a
lawyer or other person purporting to negotiate on behalf
of a defendant, has caused the plaintiff or the plaintiff’s
lawyer to reasonably believe and to rely on the belief that
(i) the defendant has been served,
(ii) liability is not or will not be contested, or
(iii) a time limit or any time period relating to the action
will not be relied on or will be waived;
(b) if an order for substitutional service, an order dispensing
with service or an order validating service is set aside;
(c) special or extraordinary circumstances exist resulting
solely from the defendant’s conduct or from the conduct
of a person who is not a party to the action.
(2)  If an extension of time is granted under subrule (1), no further
extension of time may be granted under this rule and rule 13.5 does
not apply unless different or new circumstances described in
subrule (1) are established to the Court’s satisfaction.

commentary.text: Rule 3.27 See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 3.27. 1. Comparison with previous rule In Sanderson Estate v. Potter, 2012 ABQB 593, 2012 CarswellAlta 1645, 550 A.R. 33, Madam Justice Read said, at paragraphs 27-28: 27 As can be seen, Rule 3.27(a) carries forward the three situations that allowed for a renewal of a Statement of Claim under Rule 11(9). There is minimal change in the wording. Rule 3.27(a) continues to recognize the common law defences of waiver or estoppel or equity based on a standstill agreement. In Foster v. Robb, 2011 ABQB 776, the Court held that Rules 3.26–3.28 are similar to old Rule 11 and that the principles developed under the Former Rules have been incorporated into the requirements of Rules 3.26–3.28. That Court held further that Rules 3.26–3.28 impose a strict and mandatory limit on the service of a statement of claim and only the rare exceptions listed in Rule 3.27 alter the limit on service. 28 Rule 3.27 also contains two new circumstances in which the renewal of a statement of claim will be allowed: when an order for substitutional service, an order dispensing with service or an order validating service is set aside (Rule 3.27(1)(b)) and when “special” or “extraordinary” circumstances exist resulting solely from the defendant's conduct or from the conduct of a person who is not a party to the action (Rule 3.27(1)(c)). Madam Justice Read noted that the general exception set out in R. 3.27(1)(c) was not in the previous rule. She said, at paragraphs 36–46: 36 There remains, however, the “general exception” set out in Rule 3.27(1)(c). This provision was not included in the Former Rules and there has been little judicial consideration of it as yet. From my research, it appears that only two reported cases have considered this section. 37 In Nixon v. Timms, op cit a process server swore in an affidavit of service that he had personally served the defendant, Timms. At later viva voce proceedings, the process server swore that the person he served had identified himself at the door as “Michael”, the first name of Mr. Timms and that he had confirmed the identity of Mr. Timms with an unnamed neighbour. The person actually served, denied under oath having said anything of the sort to the process server and had a specific recall of the process server's attendance, and told him he was not Mr. Timms. Timms testified that he was not served and was, in fact, out of the country at the time. The Court disbelieved the process server and accepted instead the other evidence, finding that the process server had sworn a false affidavit. At para 47, the Court concluded: Rule 3.27 specifically contemplates the kind of unusual and entirely unanticipated consequence of a false affidavit being sworn upon which an entire case would stand or fall. It is such an unusual and extraordinary circumstance that one could hardly imagine occurring, let alone expect it to arise shortly after the implementation of Rule 3.27 which provides the obvious remedy in order that neither party be prejudiced. 38 On the other hand, in Vanden Brink v. Russell, 2012 ABQB 523, in comments that must be seen as obiter, given his disposition of the case, a Master of the Court of Queen's Bench said this in respect to Rule 3.27: 22 With the current unsettled state of the law as to onus, a plaintiff obtaining a default judgment faces the prospect of that judgment later being set aside based on a bare denial of service by the defendant. The consequence of setting aside the judgment may be that time for service of the statement of claim will have elapsed, and the cause of action now lost due to limitations issues. While Rule 3.27(1)(b) allows for the time for service of a statement of claim to be extended where, for example, an order for substitutional service is later set aside, there is no provision to extend the time for service of a statement of claim where proof of service, upon which a default judgment has been issued, is later rejected. 39 The purpose of the Rule is to ensure that a plaintiff takes timely action in pursuing a claim and to encourage expeditious litigation. In this case, although the Statement of Claim was issued only shortly before the expiry of the relevant limitation period, the Plaintiff did take timely action in serving it. The lack of service was not caused by any inaction on the part of the Plaintiff, who relied upon the affidavit of service of his agent the process server. It was the mistake or negligence of the process server, and the reliance of the Plaintiff on this error, that resulted in Reimer not being served while the Statement of Claim was in force. However, although the parties are agreed that the affidavit of service is erroneous, unlike the situation in Nixon v. Timms, where the Court found that the affidavit of service was fraudulent, there is no evidence here of what actually happened. Nor can it be said that the circumstances of this case arose from the Defendant's conduct or the conduct of a person who is not a party to the action. 40 However, although the process server is the agent of the Plaintiff, that does not make him a party to the action. I interpret the words “person who is not a party to the action” in Rule 327(1)(c) to include a process server who has mistakenly or negligently filed an erroneous affidavit of service. 41 Process servers are commonly used in situations such as this, where an action is commenced and personal service is required. The use of a process server is, therefore, hardly a special or extraordinary circumstance. Nor, I suspect, is it a special or extraordinary circumstance for a process server to have difficulty with positive identification of someone he or she serves. The question is, do the circumstances here constitute a “special” or “extraordinary” circumstance as contemplated in Rule 327(1)(c)? 42 The Shorter Oxford English Dictionary, (5th ed) Oxford, England: Oxford University Press, 2002, defines “extraordinary” as “out of the usual or regular course or order; special”, “of a kind not usually met with, exceptional; now esp so exceptional as to provoke astonishment”. It defines “special” as “exceptional in quality or degree; unusual, out of the ordinary”. 43 In Nixon v. Timms, the process server was found to have lied on an affidavit of service. As the Court there found, such a circumstance is so rare as to be almost unimaginable. Such a circumstance is clearly “extraordinary”. Here, as in Nixon, the affidavit of service is incorrect. However, it is false and not fraudulent. The process server was mistaken in his affidavit. He did not serve Reimer as he swore he did. Although a mistaken affidavit is not the same as a fraudulent one, the mistake here could not have occurred through mere inadvertence. In the absence of any evidence that someone misled the process server, I must conclude that the process server was at least, careless and perhaps negligent. In my view, the mistaken affidavit sworn by the process server and relied upon by the Plaintiff, is a “special” circumstance such as contemplated by the Rule. 44 A decision to permit the renewal of an expired statement of claim is a discretionary one and involves some latitude. As stated by Burrows, J. in Syvenky v. Woo, 2003 ABQB 764: 14 Of course, when the situation described in Rule 11(9) exists the jurisdiction to renew the statement of claim is discretionary. The exercise of the discretion will be influenced by factors such as prejudice to the defendant and carelessness by the plaintiff. In a situation where the plaintiff's belief and reliance were brought to an end soon after the statement of claim were issued by advice that liability was in dispute, the court might well decline to renew the statement of claim. On the other end of the spectrum, if the plaintiff was induced to believe until the last few days before the expiry of the statement of claim that liability would not be contested, I expect the renewal would be easily obtained. 17 It is also significant to the exercise of the discretion that Mr. Woo suffered no prejudice as a result of Mr. Syvenky's failure to serve the statement of claim in the year. The statement of claim was in fact served, albeit substitutionally after it appeared Mr. Woo was avoiding service, within 15 months of the issuance of the statement of claim. If application had been made for a renewal of the statement of claim before the expiry of the first 12 months it would have likely been granted. The service which was effected was within the 3 months of the renewal which would have been granted. 45 The Ontario Court of Appeal has also made it clear that the key issue is prejudice to the defendant when dealing with applications to extend the time for service of an expired statement of claim. In Chiarelli et al v. Wiens (2000) 46 O.R. (3d) 780, Laskin J.A., speaking for the court, said this: 17 The court should not fix in advance rules or guidelines when an extension should be refused. Effect of Negotiations on Service—Standstill Agreements I agree with the reasons for judgment of Mr. Justice Major. When the insurers wrote to the appellant's lawyers asking that they take no further steps without ample notice to the insurers, they waived their right to rely on the failure of the appellant's lawyers to serve the renewed statement of claim during its currency. The copy of the renewed statement of claim which was delivered to the insurers by the respondent's widow showed clearly that the renewal was for three months from March 3, 1988. They knew, therefore, that it would expire on June 3, 1988. And they knew that it had not been served on the respondent. However, as late as December 19, 1988, they made an offer of settlement, which the appellant rejected. I find in this conduct confirmation of the insurers' waiver of their right to rely on the failure of the appellant's lawyers to effect proper service of the statement of claim during its currency. Cyre-Wills v. Couture (1992), 1 Alta. L.R. (3d) 209 (C.A.), at 211-12, per Hetherington J.A. In Martinez v. Hogeweide (1998), 209 A.R. 388 (C.A.), the court commented on the effect of a “standstill agreement”. At pp. 389-90 the court said: In our view not all agreements or waivers removing the need to take some step literally stop the clock so that the intervening time will be added on to the end of usual time limits… Rather, it is a matter of interpreting the correspondence or discussions in each case. . . . . . Therefore, neither the parties' words [in this case] nor equity nor necessity support a true stand-still which would automatically add the waived time to the end of the 12 months. Solicitors wishing that should say so clearly. In Dewindt v. Sandalwood Homes Ltd., 2002 ABQB 316, 2002 CarswellAlta 395, 313 A.R. 96, Clackson J. described situations in which a standstill agreement would be found. At pp. 102-103, His Lordship said: A standstill agreement is a peculiar feature of Alberta jurisprudence which is generally found only in cases where a Statement of Claim has been issued but not served within the time limited by the Rules of Court. Generally, a standstill agreement is found in the following circumstances: (a) where a Defendant has asked the Plaintiff not to take further steps on an issued claim while settlement discussions are ongoing; or (b) where a Statement of Claim has not been served, although not at the request of the Defendant and the time for service of the Statement of Claim has expired while settlement discussions were ongoing and settlement discussions continued after that expiry. . . . . . It seems to me that notwithstanding some rather loose language used from time to time in considering standstill agreements, such an agreement might be established where, by words or conduct the parties have actually or implicitly agreed to stop the clock while they talk and start the clock when they stop. A standstill agreement is not waiver because the agreement pre-dates the expiry of the time period. It pre-dates the right, interest, or privilege. A standstill agreement is not promissory estoppel because it is an agreement in the full legal sense of the word. The consideration which passes is the desire for effective, efficient, and lower cost settlements. In Kapki v. Palacz (1998), 60 Alta. L.R. (3d) 145 (Q.B.); [affirmed (1999) 228 A.R. 373 (C.A.)], Mason J. said, at p. 149: Disputed standstill agreements may well be inferred by what is said and done between the parties or by how they might otherwise conduct themselves. In Wasyleshko v. Chamakese (1999), 228 A.R. 384 (C.A.), the Court of Appeal, at pp. 385-86, said: A standstill agreement obliges a plaintiff to take no further prejudicial steps in an action in consideration of ongoing settlement negotiations. Whether there is a standstill agreement and its scope are questions of fact… . . . . . … the relevant inquiry is whether the exchange of correspondence and the conduct of the parties evidences the acceptance and reliance necessary to show a standstill arrangement in respect of procedural matters pending settlement discussions. In Virji v. Kramer, 2001 ABQB 205, 2001 CarswellAlta 306, 285 A.R. 181 (Master), Master Quinn noted at p. 186: According to the Kapki decision the critical question is whether it is clear the time limits for service were not being relied on by the defendants. And at p. 387 the Court of Appeal suggested how disputes on standstill agreements might be avoided: We think it important to signal to the profession that when a standstill agreement is entered into, it would be preferable to describe it as such, and to state precisely what steps in the litgation process are waived or suspended pending the exploration of settlement. 12. Timing of Rule 3.27 Application No exact period of time can be prescribed within which a court may allow an application under rule 11(9). The court has a discretion in granting an order renewing a statement of claim and in exercising that discretion the court must look at the facts of the case. The application for an order to renew the statement of claim must be brought within a reasonable period of time having regard to all the circumstances. It would seem prudent in these cases once negotiations break down and counsel is put on notice that service is required that they will within a reasonable period of time serve the defendants or make application under rule 11(9) for renewing the statement of claim. Difficulty in locating the defendants or difficulty in serving the defendants, once located, should trigger an immediate application for an order under rule 11(9). Lundrigan v. Kundert (2001), 290 A.R. 160 (Master) at 165-166, per Master Laycock. Renewal under Rule 3.26 Operates Against All Defendants In Elizabeth Diane Yackel v. Sandra Snape/Acquest Financial Services Inc. and John Snape/A.P.I. Financial Group Inc. and Sentinel Life Management Corporation, Q.B., Doc. 0101-04928, 30th January 2006 (not reported), Lutz, J distinguished between a renewal granted under Rule 11(9) (see current R. 3.27(1)(a)) and a renewal granted under Rule 11(2) (see current R. 3.26). Under the latter, his Lordship agreed with this statement put to him in submissions: “Rule 11(2) therefore should be interpreted such that the renewal order made under that subrule operates as against all defendants.” (See p. 26 of the Reasons for Judgment). 13. Purpose of Rule 3.27 In Meyer v. Vasiu, 2002 ABQB 182, 2002 CarswellAlta 208, 313 A.R. 315, the plaintiff applied for a renewal order on the basis that an insurer had made a payment to the plaintiff pursuant to “an inter-company agreement between insurers known as the ‘fault chart’”. In dismissing the application, Belzil J. said, at pp. 317-318: I accept that the solicitor representing the Plaintiffs was unaware of the “fault chart,” but in my view, nothing turns on this. The real issue is whether or not the payments made by the insurer, for whatever reason, on the wording in Rule 11(9) caused the solicitor to reasonably believe that liability was not going to be contested. It is significant that the payments made by the insurer pre-dated the issuance of the Statement of Claim by more than one year and thus can be considered to be remote in time from the issuance of the Statement of Claim. In addition, it is uncontroverted that the solicitor for the Plaintiffs made no attempt to contact the insurer after issuance of the Statement of Claim, notwithstanding that the solicitor had previously corresponded with an employee of the insurer and that the insurer had forwarded correspondence denying liability, which correspondence was never retracted. There is no evidence that the solicitor for the Plaintiffs ever addressed his mind to the issue of serving the Statement of Claim; thus it cannot be argued that the solicitor made a conscious decision not to serve the Statement of Claim on the basis of payments previously made. On its plain wording, Rule 11(9) makes reference to a plaintiff or a plaintiff's lawyer. Surely the subjective and objective standards of what constitutes a reasonable belief are significantly higher for a lawyer compared to an unrepresented plaintiff. The Court can take judicial notice of the fact that payments are made by parties and their insurers for a variety of reasons, and there is no authority for the proposition that every payment made by a party or its insurer constitutes an admission of liability express or implied. The reality is that payments are often made on a nuisance value basis to avoid litigation. Moreover, a payment made for property damage surely does not mean that a party or its insurer thereafter agrees to pay damages for personal injury and associated claims, particularly bearing in mind that the latter amounts are often significantly larger. It is simply not reasonable for a lawyer to believe that payments for property damage, without more, are equivalent to an admission of liability or an undertaking not to contest liability. At the time the “fault chart” payments were made, there is no evidence that the insurer was or could have been aware of the quantum of the claims the Plaintiffs would be making, or that the Plaintiffs were in fact going to proceed with claims given that the insurer had denied liability up to that point in its correspondence. Up to that point, the solicitor for the Plaintiffs had not forwarded any information regarding the quantum of the claims being made by his clients. As such, the payments made by the insurer cannot be characterized as extensions of any settlement discussions which had taken place up to that point when in fact no such discussions had taken place, or from the insurer's perspective may not have even been contemplated. The mischief which Rule 11(9) is designed to address is that of lulling someone into a false sense of security and acting to their detriment by way of not serving a Statement of Claim. Rule 11(9) does not alleviate the need for a solicitor who files pleadings to be diligent in serving the same bearing in mind the requirement of Rule 11(1) to serve the Statement of Claim within 12 months. On these facts, the Plaintiffs' solicitor did not have cause to reasonably believe that liability was not going to be contested and thus should have served the statement of claim. Accordingly, the application pursuant to Rule 11(9) is dismissed with costs. In Syvenky v. Woo, 2003 ABQB 764, 2003 CarswellAlta 1280, 24 Alta. L.R. (4th) 292, a self-represented plaintiff in a motor vehicle accident claim believed, as a result of those acting for the defendant, that the defendant admitted liability. That belief ended 9 months after the issuance of the statement of claim when the defendant's insurance adjuster wrote to the plaintiff and indicated that all defences, including liability, would be pursued by the defendant. The statement of claim was served pursuant to an order for substitutional service 15 months after the claim was issued. In granting an application to renew the statement of claim, Burrows J., at pp. 295-296, said: Rule 11 creates a limitation period. Limitation provisions are to be construed strictly. “Before a person should be deprived of his or her cause of action, the language in the limiting statute should be clear and unambiguous.” (Conrad J.A., in Campbell Estate v. Fang, [1994] 9 W.W.R. 208, ¶ 10.) Rule 11(9) contains nothing to suggest that the plaintiff's belief and reliance that liability is not contested must exist at the time the statement of claim expires in order for the Court to renew the statement of claim. It says only that the belief and reliance must have been induced before the statement of claim expired. It if had been intended that the state of belief described in Rule 11(9) should exist at the time the statement of claim expired, one would expect to find words to that effect in the rule. The rule must not be construed as confining the jurisdiction to renew more narrowly than a fair reading of its words requires. Of course, when the situation described in Rule 11(9) exists the jurisdiction to renew the statement of claim is discretionary. The exercise of the discretion will be influenced by factors such as prejudice to the defendant and carelessness by the plaintiff. In a situation where the plaintiff's belief and reliance were brought to an end soon after the statement of claim was issued by advice that liability was in dispute, the court might well decline to renew the statement of claim. On the other end of the spectrum, if the plaintiff was induced to believe until the last few days before the expiry of the statement of claim that liability would not be contested, I expect the renewal would be easily obtained. 14. No Extension When Process Server Swore False Affidavit of Service In Nixon v. Timms, 2013 ABCA 84, 2013 CarswellAlta 259, 544 A.R. 21, the Plaintiff unwittingly relied on a falsely sworn affidavit of service. The Court of Appeal held that service had not been effected within the required time, and that the Statement of Claim had expired and no further action could be taken under it. At paragraphs 1–6, and 8–11, the Court said: 1 THE COURT:—The issue on this appeal is a narrow one. Can Rule 3.27 of the Alberta Rules of Court apply in this case to revive a claim that expired under R. 11 of the former Alberta Rules of Court? In our view, given the circumstances here, the answer is no. 2 A statement of claim was issued by Nixon, the respondent, against Timms, the appellant, on February 23, 2007 in which Nixon sought to recover money from Timms as a result of a failed real estate transaction. A process server hired by Nixon went to an Edmonton address to attempt service. The process server swore an affidavit that he had effected personal service on Timms at that address on December 20, 2007. 3 In reliance on the affidavit of service Timms was noted in default and judgment entered. In May 2011 Timms received notice of the judgment and moved to set it aside. 4 The trial judge found on the evidence before her that the statement of claim had not been served. Rather, the affidavit of service relied upon to note Timms in default had been sworn fraudulently and was not true. Timms was unaware of the claim until execution on the default judgment was attempted. The trial judge concluded that there had been no service of the statement of claim and set aside the default judgment. She declined to strike the claim or otherwise find it to have expired, declared that service had now been properly effected and ordered the defendant to file a defence within 20 days. Timms appeals. 5 The appellant submits that the trial judge erred in determining that an unserved statement of claim under the old rules was merely suspended, in applying the new rules of court, and in extending the time for service of the claim. We agree. 6 Under R. 11 of the former rules of court, this claim would have expired on February 23, 2008. Rule 11 did not allow for the extension of time to serve in these particular circumstances. Rule 11(1) provided that a statement of claim was in force for 12 months after it was filed. Thereafter, the rules deemed the claim to have expired. Under Rr. 11(b) and (c) the plaintiff could apply for one three month extension at any time before the 12 months had passed. No such extension was sought nor would R. 11(9) have permitted its renewal thereafter. Nevertheless, the trial judge concluded that the claim “was not a nullity” and could be renewed for an additional three months under the provisions of the new rules of court. In our view, her conclusion is incorrect. … 8 In this case, the statement of claim was never properly served. No renewal of the claim was sought while it was in force and R. 11(9), which provided for renewal in certain extraordinary circumstances, does not cover this situation. Accordingly, the statement of claim expired on its face in February 2008. The statement of claim was not suspended. The statement of claim could not be renewed under any aspect of then R. 11. When the statement of claim expired, the respondent was barred from taking any further action on the claim. Accordingly, in these circumstances the new Alberta Rules of Court cannot retroactively revive an action that expired in 2008. 9 Our view is reinforced when considered in the context of the respondent's submission that the claim had not “expired” but was suspended or capable of being renewed under R. 3.27 “at any time”. Counsel fairly conceded that although the rule involved a strict test, the trial judge's interpretation of the rule would involve endless or timeless discretion to restore a claim. In effect, the rule could be applied in these same circumstances in the year 2040 or beyond. 10 We do not accept that the drafters of R. 3.27 intended this broad a discretion or the perpetual ability to renew expired claims. We note, however, that in considering whether extraordinary circumstances exist in a given case or whether to exercise a discretion under the rule, regard must be had to the policy considerations in the Limitations Act, RSA 2000, c. L-12 and any prejudice arising as a result of the expiration of a particular limitation period. 11 The appeal must be allowed. The statement of claim expired in February 2008 and no further action can be taken under it.
